title: XSS and unsafe HTML insertion
learningObjectives: Explain xss and unsafe html insertion and apply secure, accessible, maintainable browser practices.

understand.concept: Cross-site scripting (XSS) occurs when attacker-controlled data is interpreted as executable content in a user's browser. Injection paths include unsafe HTML insertion, dangerous URL contexts, and script-capable attributes. Context-aware output handling and a restrictive Content Security Policy reduce risk.
understand.whyItMatters: XSS can expose account data, perform actions as the user, or alter page content. Treat API data, user text, URLs, and stored content as untrusted.
understand.analogy: XSS is like allowing a stranger to write instructions on a public control panel that other users will follow.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy is simplified; browser security, accessibility, and performance rules depend on platform behaviour and server configuration.

explain.narrative: The content is displayed as text and is not interpreted as an HTML element. Never demonstrate active payloads against real systems.

examples.explanation: The content is displayed as text and is not interpreted as an HTML element. Never demonstrate active payloads against real systems.
examples.expectedOutput: Browser console or UI output demonstrates the security or reliability principle.

practise.guidedTask: Identify unsafe output contexts in a sample page and replace string-based markup insertion with safe DOM APIs.
practise.independentTask: Review a small browser feature for security, accessibility, performance, and lifecycle risks. Add a fallback and document the server-side controls required.
hints: Treat all browser and network input as untrusted.
Use exact origin checks and least privilege.
Measure performance and clean up resources.

questions.prompt: What is a core prevention practice for rendering untrusted text?
options: Use textContent or safe DOM construction
questions.answer: Use textContent or safe DOM construction
questions.explanation: Treat untrusted data as text and avoid parsing it as HTML.

questions.prompt: What is a sound browser engineering principle?
options: Defence in depth, least privilege, and usable fallbacks
Assume all browser features are always available
questions.answer: Defence in depth, least privilege, and usable fallbacks
questions.explanation: Secure and reliable interfaces combine trusted server enforcement with careful client behaviour.
